Guide for Model Developers

Source: vignettes/developer-guide.Rmd
developer-guide.Rmd

Overview

This guide explains how to make your model available for independent external validation using evaluatr. Independent evaluators will be able to run secure_model_validation() in their own datasets, without you ever seeing their patient data and without them ever seeing your model’s coefficients.

You will need:

  1. A private GitHub repository to host the model specification file
  2. The evaluatr package installed locally to generate that file
  3. A developer account — just your GitHub username

This takes approximately 30 minutes to set up for the first model, and much less for subsequent ones.

Step 1: Create a private GitHub repository

If you do not already have a GitHub account, create one at github.com. Then create a new repository:

  • Set the visibility to Private
  • Choose a clear, memorable name (e.g. my-clinical-models)
  • Do not initialise with a README

Your repository will hold one or more model specifications. The required folder structure is:

my-clinical-models/
├── model_v1/
│   └── model_v1_specification.json
└── model_v2/
    └── model_v2_specification.json

The folder name (e.g. model_v1) becomes the model_id that evaluators will use. The specification file must be named {model_id}_specification.json.

Step 2: Install evaluatr and generate your model specification

The register_model() function creates the protected model specification file and registers the model with the evaluatr registry. Both steps happen in a single call and must complete before any evaluator can validate the model.

devtools::install_github("JoieEnsor/evaluatr")
library(evaluatr)

Example A: Logistic regression (DVT diagnosis model)

The DVT example dataset included with the package spans seven studies. Studies 1-5 are used here for model development; studies 6-7 are reserved for external validation.

dvt_path <- system.file("extdata", "dvt_example.csv", package = "evaluatr")
dvt_data <- read.csv(dvt_path)

# Development set: studies 1-5
dvt_dev <- dvt_data[dvt_data$study %in% 1:5, ]

# Fit a logistic regression model
dvt_fit <- glm(dvt ~ male + ab_ddimer + calf_diff + vein_distension +
                     malignancy + immobile,
               data = dvt_dev, family = binomial)

# Generate the protected model specification file
register_model(
  model           = dvt_fit,
  model_id        = "dvt_v1",
  developer_id    = "your-github-username",    # your GitHub username
  model_name      = "DVT Diagnosis Model v1",
  description     = paste(
    "Logistic regression for DVT diagnosis. Developed in studies 1-5",
    "of the simulated DVT example dataset.",
    "Predictors: male, ab_ddimer, calf_diff, vein_distension, malignancy, immobile."
  ),
  developer_name  = "Your Name",
  developer_email = "you@institution.ac.uk",
  output_dir      = "dvt_v1"
)

This writes dvt_v1/dvt_v1_specification.json. The coefficient values are protected; the file is safe to host in your GitHub repository.

Example B: Cox proportional hazards model (breast cancer relapse) 

library(survival)

bc_path <- system.file("extdata", "bc_survival_example.csv",
                       package = "evaluatr")
bc_data <- read.csv(bc_path)
bc_dev  <- bc_data[bc_data$val == 0, ]

# Fit a Cox model
cox_fit <- coxph(Surv(rf, rfi) ~ age + nodes + pr + er + hormon,
                 data = bc_dev, x = TRUE)

# Extract baseline survival at 5 and 10 years (60 and 120 months)
bh     <- basehaz(cox_fit, centered = FALSE)
S0_60  <- exp(-bh$hazard[which.min(abs(bh$time - 60))])
S0_120 <- exp(-bh$hazard[which.min(abs(bh$time - 120))])

register_model(
  model            = cox_fit,
  model_id         = "bc_cox_v1",
  developer_id     = "your-github-username",
  model_name       = "Breast Cancer Relapse-Free Survival Model",
  description      = paste(
    "Cox PH model for relapse-free survival in breast cancer.",
    "Developed in the training set (val == 0) of the bc_survival_example dataset.",
    "Predictors: age, nodes, pr, er, hormon."
  ),
  model_parameters = list(
    timepoints        = c(60, 120),
    baseline_survival = c(S0_60, S0_120)
  ),
  developer_name  = "Your Name",
  developer_email = "you@institution.ac.uk",
  output_dir      = "bc_cox_v1"
)

For Cox models, model_parameters must include timepoints and baseline_survival so that evaluatr can produce predicted survival probabilities at specific time-points.

Example C: Model with embedded pre-processing

If your model uses derived or transformed predictors, you can embed the transformation so that evaluators provide raw data with no additional steps required on their side. Supply an R code string as the preprocessing argument:

# A Cox model using log-transformed pr and er
cox_log_fit <- coxph(Surv(rf, rfi) ~ age + nodes + log(pr + 1) + log(er + 1),
                     data = bc_dev, x = TRUE)

bh2     <- basehaz(cox_log_fit, centered = FALSE)
S0_60b  <- exp(-bh2$hazard[which.min(abs(bh2$time - 60))])
S0_120b <- exp(-bh2$hazard[which.min(abs(bh2$time - 120))])

register_model(
  model            = cox_log_fit,
  model_id         = "bc_cox_log_v1",
  developer_id     = "your-github-username",
  model_name       = "BC Survival Model (log biomarkers)",
  preprocessing    = "
    validation_data$`log(pr + 1)` <- log(validation_data$pr + 1)
    validation_data$`log(er + 1)` <- log(validation_data$er + 1)
  ",
  model_parameters = list(
    timepoints        = c(60, 120),
    baseline_survival = c(S0_60b, S0_120b)
  ),
  developer_name  = "Your Name",
  developer_email = "you@institution.ac.uk",
  output_dir      = "bc_cox_log_v1"
)

The preprocessing code is run on validation_data (the evaluator’s dataset) before prediction. The code must create any derived columns in place. It has access only to validation_data.

If you do not embed preprocessing, the variable names in variables (or the coefficient names extracted from your model) must match the column names the evaluator will have in their dataset. Document any required transformations clearly in the model description.

Example D: Manual coefficient specification

If your coefficients come from a publication or software other than R, you can supply them directly:

register_model(
  coefficients = c("(Intercept)" = -3.2,
                   ab_ddimer     =  1.8,
                   calf_diff     =  1.1,
                   vein_distension = 0.9),
  model_type   = "logistic",
  model_id     = "dvt_published_v1",
  developer_id = "your-github-username",
  model_name   = "Published DVT Score (manual)",
  outcome_type = "binary",
  variables    = c("ab_ddimer", "calf_diff", "vein_distension"),
  description  = "Coefficients from Smith et al. (2024), Table 2.",
  developer_name  = "Your Name",
  developer_email = "you@institution.ac.uk",
  output_dir   = "dvt_published_v1"
)

Keeping a model private while a paper is under review

Set public_listing = FALSE to register the model without it appearing in the public directory. You can still issue tokens to peer reviewers or journal editors. Update to public_listing = TRUE by re-running register_model() with a new model_id when ready to publish.

Step 3: Verify your model specification

Before sharing with any evaluator, confirm that evaluatr’s predictions match your own. Because secure_model_validation() returns shuffled predictions, sort both sets before comparing:

# Validate in your own development data using your own full-access PAT
result_check <- secure_model_validation(
  repo_owner      = "your-github-username",
  repo_name       = "my-clinical-models",
  model_id        = "dvt_v1",
  github_token    = Sys.getenv("GITHUB_PAT"),   # your own full-access PAT
  validation_data = dvt_dev,
  outcome         = "dvt"
)

# Your own predictions (unsorted)
manual_probs <- predict(dvt_fit, type = "response")

# Sort both and compare
max(abs(sort(manual_probs) - sort(result_check$shuffled_predictions)))
# Should be < 1e-6

A difference larger than 1e-4 indicates a coefficient or transformation mismatch. Check variable names and ordering carefully.

Step 4: Upload to GitHub

Upload the generated file to your private repository at the path:

<model_id>/<model_id>_specification.json

For example, for model_id = "dvt_v1":

my-clinical-models/
└── dvt_v1/
    └── dvt_v1_specification.json

You can do this via the GitHub web interface (drag and drop into the correct folder) or using the command line:

git add dvt_v1/dvt_v1_specification.json
git commit -m "Add DVT v1 model specification"
git push

Step 5: Issue access tokens to evaluators

For each evaluator (or group of evaluators), create a fine-grained personal access token:

  1. Go to GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens
  2. Click Generate new token
  3. Under Repository access, select Only select repositories and choose your model repository
  4. Under Permissions, set Contents to Read-only (no other permissions are needed)
  5. Set an appropriate Expiration — we recommend a short-lived token
  6. Generate and copy the token

Send the token to the evaluator along with your GitHub username, repository name, and model ID.

Issue a unique token per evaluator. This lets you revoke access for a specific evaluator without affecting others and creates an audit trail of who has accessed the model specification.

Repository structure summary 

my-clinical-models/                          ← private GitHub repository
├── dvt_v1/
│   └── dvt_v1_specification.json            ← model_id = "dvt_v1"
└── bc_cox_v1/
    └── bc_cox_v1_specification.json          ← model_id = "bc_cox_v1"

The evaluator calls:

secure_model_validation(
  repo_owner      = "your-github-username",
  repo_name       = "my-clinical-models",
  model_id        = "dvt_v1",
  github_token    = "token_you_issued",
  validation_data = their_data,
  outcome         = "dvt"
)

Checklist before sharing with evaluators

    • Your GitHub username (repo_owner)
    • The repository name (repo_name)
    • The model ID (model_id)
    • Which variables their dataset must contain (variables field in the model description)
    • Any transformations they need to apply (if not embedded in preprocessing)
